Workflow is running in the background (`/workflows` to watch live). Here's what I dispatched and the two judgment calls I made along the way.

**Corpus reality check.** Your `~/.claude` is a symlink to `~/.claude2` — the transcripts are there: 1158 sessions, 754 of them lobu. Codex has 1.2GB of rollouts, Grok 1.8GB of sessions. Gemini and opencode I dropped: their 3.1GB and 57MB are almost entirely `antigravity` caches, browser profiles, and `node_modules`, with no conversation corpus worth mining. Not going to send agents to grind through that and report back nothing.

**Twelve agents, not twenty.** Your session config caps workflows at ~15, and the corpus genuinely splits into about eight distinct mining seams. Past that, agents start re-reading each other's files and you pay tokens for duplicate findings — which cuts against the token-efficiency half of what you asked for. The eight miners run in parallel, then up to 24 candidate findings get adversarially verified (each verifier is told to *refute*, and to default to "does not hold up" on thin evidence), then one synthesizer ranks what survives.

**On the Workflow tool:** I'm treating your "you can use workflow tool" as a one-turn override. Your memory has that rule reaffirmed three times, so I've left it standing — say the word if you want it revised permanently.

Two design choices worth flagging, since they shape what comes back:

- Miners are instructed to read `AGENTS.md` first and **skip anything already encoded there**. The value is in what you *haven't* written down yet, not a re-derivation of your existing invariants.
- Findings are ranked by recurrence. A mistake that happened once is noise; one that bit three separate sessions is a missing guard. Only recurring-or-high-value findings get spent on verification.

The repo-audit agents (multi-replica state, fail-open authz, test trustworthiness) are read-only — no edits, no worktrees, nothing touched on disk.

When it lands I'll give you the ranked report, then write the durable cross-session lessons to memory as you asked. I'll show you the proposed memory entries before writing them rather than silently appending to an index that's already ~130 lines.

One caveat on confidence: transcript mining surfaces *claims*, and the verify pass checks them against `origin/main`, but a finding that survives is still "supported by evidence," not "reproduced." I'll mark anything resting on thin evidence as such rather than presenting the whole report at uniform confidence.

## Do these three first

**1. Fix the inert-guard class, starting with the live instance.** `packages/server/src/auth/__tests__/access-model-cross-check.test.ts:130` has `if (runtimeTier === null) continue;`. Instrumenting the committed file and running `bunx vitest run` gives `{"noTool":41,"manage":9,"silentlySkipped":25,"total":128}` with `Tests 3 passed` — 75 of 128 SDK methods are never asserted while CI reports the authz drift guard green. Fix: replace the silent skip with an enumerated allowlist snapshot of the 25 currently-skipped methods so any *new* skip fails the build. Do not assert `silentlySkipped === 0`; the file's own comment documents a legitimate handler-`readOnly` fallback the static test can't reproduce, so a bare zero fails on day one. Then add to AGENTS.md: a guard with a `continue`/early-return skip path must assert its own coverage count, and a mutation test must be verified to have *landed* (re-read the file, confirm red) — `feedback_mutation_test_new_tests.md`'s `perl -0pi -e` recipe silently no-ops on whitespace mismatch, which is exactly how session 81ba9cd8 was fooled into "passing" a mutation that was never applied. Same class in five other subsystems (566d20f5 reconcile, d905228d approval, 54ce9add connector ACL, 50c81846 null no-op). **Highest value, ~1 hour, and it is wrong right now.** Confidence: high — reproduced live on origin/main.

**2. Add the "absence is not proven by grep" rule to AGENTS.md.** Right now `~/Code/lobu` is on `feat/activity-memory-split` and local `main` is 14 commits behind `origin/main`, so any plain grep there reads a feature branch. Seven sessions made a wrong call from this; 59170af4 (2026-07-28) drove a wrong orphaned-script deletion off a "zero callers" grep against a checkout 20 commits stale. Fix, under "Agent workflow": *Absence is never proven by `grep`/`find` on a working tree. To prove code does not exist, run `git fetch -q origin && git grep <pattern> origin/main` — the fetch is load-bearing since `origin/main` itself goes stale. Applies to every existence check, including the deletion-evidence rule.* Put it in AGENTS.md, not global CLAUDE.md: several incidents were in dispatched subagents that never see the global file. **Five minutes, prevents a whole failure mode.** Confidence: high.

**3. Extend the screenshot hook to cover `Read`.** Across 1209 transcripts, `Read` produced 67.1 MB of base64 image data over 239 results (274 KB avg) vs `mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer` at 77.7 MB over 1058 (71.8 KB avg) — 4x the per-image cost because the MCP tool downscales and `Read` doesn't. The regime change is the tell: before 2026-07-15 (when `prefer-dom-over-screenshot.sh` shipped) `computer` was 90.7% of image bytes and `Read` 5.3%; after, `Read` is 83.6% and `computer` 9.3%. The guard worked and the cost migrated to the uncovered path. `~/.claude/settings.json` matches PreToolUse only on `mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer|browser_batch`, never `Read`. Fix: extend the same hook to match `Read`, inspect `file_path`, and emit a non-blocking nudge for `.png/.jpg` over ~150 KB pointing at `sips -Z 900 <in> --out <scratchpad>/small.png`. This directly supersedes `feedback_session_context_bloat_habits.md`, which ranked `Read` at 9% and "negligible" — now inverted. **Honest caveat on the cost framing:** the damage is transcript bloat and compaction pressure (a 23 MB session file), not token billing — a 3456x1730 PNG is ~1.6k tokens after Anthropic's downscale, not the ~170k a naive text heuristic suggests. Also 100 of the 165 oversized reads are one landing-repo video-frame session where the pixels *are* the deliverable; exempt that. Confidence: high on the measurement, medium on the size of the win.

## 1. Bug-free / prod-ready

**Org-scoping on composite-PK tables is fixed one sibling at a time.** `agents_pkey PRIMARY KEY (organization_id, id)` (baseline.sql; same for `agent_users`, `grants`, `agent_secrets`, `conversations`), so `lobu-builder` shares one id across ~20 orgs. content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

Design plan before I build.

**Read:** utilitarian, not editorial. This is an audit report a maintainer will scan for what's broken and act on — closer to a dashboard than an essay. So: information design over flourish, state encoded in form, summary before detail. No hero.

**Subject world:** transcript forensics. 43 claims went in, 7 came out. The refutation is the story, so the page should make survived-vs-refuted legible at a glance — a verdict ledger, not a listicle.

**Color:** ground `#12131A` / paper `#FAF9F7`; neutrals biased cool-slate toward the accent. Accent `#3B5BDB` (indigo — reads instrument, not alarm). Semantic and separate from accent: confirmed `#2F855A`, caveat `#B7791F`, refuted `#9B2C2C`.

**Type:** display `Newsreader` (a slightly literary serif — this is testimony from a corpus), body system-ui stack at 65ch, data in `ui-monospace` with tabular-nums for the counts and file:line refs. No webfont URLs — CSP would silently fall back.

**Layout:** funnel strip up top (43→24→7), then three ranked findings as severity-striped cards, then the sections, then a distinct refuted ledger. Confidence rendered as a chip on every claim, since the report's honesty about thin evidence is the most useful thing in it.

Session audit · 2026-07-29

What eight thousand sessions actually say about shipping bugs

Eight agents mined the Claude, Codex and Grok transcript corpora plus the lobu repo for recurring failure modes, wasted context, and unfinished work. Forty-three claims came back. Seven survived being argued with.

33 agents 2.25M subagent tokens 14 min wall-clock 8 GB corpus 1,158 Claude sessions

The refutation is the result

Every candidate finding was handed to a verifier told to refute it, checking against committed code on origin/main rather than the working tree, and to default to “does not hold up” on thin evidence. Most did not hold up.

43 Mined Raw claims from 8 parallel miners
24 Verified Recurring or high-value enough to spend tokens on
17 Refuted 71% failure rate — stale, inflated, or already fixed
7 Survived Evidence held against committed code

Do these three first

The only findings that are both cheap and currently producing wrong outcomes.

01

An authz guard is inert right now

Verified on origin/main High confidence ~1 hour

packages/server/src/auth/__tests__/access-model-cross-check.test.ts:130 contains if (runtimeTier === null) continue;. Instrumenting the committed file yields 75 of 128 SDK methods never asserted — 41 with no tool, 9 manage, 25 silently skipped — while the suite reports three tests passed and CI marks the authz drift guard green. The line was confirmed present on origin/main by direct inspection, not inference.

The same shape appears in five other subsystems: reconcile, approval, connector ACL, and a null no-op path.

Fix Replace the silent skip with an enumerated allowlist snapshot of the 25 currently-skipped methods, so any new skip fails the build. Do not assert silentlySkipped === 0 — the file’s own comment documents a legitimate handler readOnly fallback the static test cannot reproduce, so a bare zero fails on day one.
02

Absence is never proven by grep on a working tree

High confidence 5 minutes 7 sessions affected

The main checkout currently sits on feat/activity-memory-split with local main fourteen commits behind origin, so a plain grep there reads a feature branch. Seven sessions made a wrong call from this. One on 2026-07-28 drove a wrong orphaned-script deletion off a “zero callers” grep against a checkout twenty commits stale.

Fix Add to AGENTS.md under “Agent workflow”: to prove code does not exist, run git fetch -q origin && git grep <pattern> origin/main. The fetch is load-bearing, since origin/main itself goes stale. This belongs in AGENTS.md rather than global CLAUDE.md — several incidents were in dispatched subagents that never see the global file.
03

The screenshot hook worked, and the cost moved next door

High on measurement Medium on payoff ~30 minutes

Across 1,209 transcripts, Read produced 67.1 MB of image data over 239 results (274 KB average) against mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer at 77.7 MB over 1,058 results (71.8 KB average) — four times the per-image cost, because the browser tool downscales and Read does not.

The regime change is the tell. Before prefer-dom-over-screenshot.sh shipped on 2026-07-15, computer was 90.7% of image bytes and Read 5.3%. After, Read is 83.6% and computer 9.3%. The guard worked; the cost migrated to the path it did not cover. settings.json matches PreToolUse only on computer|browser_batch, never Read.

Fix Extend the same hook to match Read, inspect file_path, and emit a non-blocking nudge for images over ~150 KB pointing at sips -Z 900.
Honest caveat The damage is transcript bloat and compaction pressure — one session file hit 23 MB — not token billing. A full-resolution PNG costs roughly 1.6k tokens after downscale, not the ~170k a naive text heuristic implies. And 100 of the 165 oversized reads come from a single video-frame session where the pixels were the deliverable; exempt that case.

Also found

Real, but either slower to act on or resting on softer evidence.

Org-scoping is being fixed one sibling at a time

Design rule, not open vuln 8 PRs / 3 months

agents_pkey PRIMARY KEY (organization_id, id) — same for agent_users, grants, agent_secrets, conversations — so lobu-builder shares one id across roughly twenty orgs. Eight merged PRs in disjoint files across three months: #1771, #1772, #1779, #1783, #1784, #1848, #2176, #2181. The body of #2181 opens “Problem (sibling of #2176)” — the grep-the-class rule failing after it already existed.

Fix Make organizationId a required parameter at the resolver seam, as #1848 and #1784 each did by hand. Notably the obvious CI guard would not work: the leaks live in ambient org resolution and TypeScript signatures, not tagged SQL templates, and a regex check in check-security-patterns.sh would fire on 44 non-test agent_id matches.
Correction carried forward #1848’s cross-tenant DELETE was not a live primitive — existing notes already record it as largely a false alarm, since the fenced handler was dead code. Treat this as a design rule rather than an open vulnerability.

CI logs get re-downloaded instead of saved once

High confidence 21 sessions · 170 refetches

One session hit the same job nine times in 105 seconds, ending with a full remote re-download of a 12,500-line log to read thirty lines by offset. Another made five calls on one job over 2m23s with grep -a appearing only on the fourth attempt — proving the encoding was never inspected. Still happening as of 2026-07-28. Nothing in AGENTS.md, GOTCHAS.md, or memory covers it.

Fix New “CI triage” section in docs/GOTCHAS.md: fetch once to a file; use --log not --log-failed, which is empty for non-test job failures like check-drift and publish-packages and is what forces the second fetch; grep needs -a because logs are timestamp and ANSI prefixed.

Four programs sit on unverified prod

High confidence 1 line in AGENTS.md

Four memory entries carry an “OWED prod verify” line and no closure: the MCP client activity surface (marked COMPLETE on 2026-07-28), the prod MCP reliability sweep, approval live-state, and multi-replica interaction cards.

The diagnosis worth pushing back on: it is not that the 30–60 minute Flux lag outlives the session. That was already solved on 2026-07-14, when a self-rescheduling wakeup polled the deployed SHA, ran the live check on landing, and wrote the result back to memory. The pattern exists and is simply written down nowhere, so it gets applied inconsistently.

Fix One line in “Ship a change”, after the merge step: when a merged PR touches a prod-visible surface, set a self-rescheduling wakeup carrying the rollout gate, and write the result back to memory. Do not build a prod-verify issue queue or cron agent — memory already carries closures elsewhere.

Refuted

Seventeen claims failed verification. These three matter most, because each would have sent you to fix something that is not broken.

make review is being run as a find-fix loop
The repeat runs span separate worktrees and separate PRs. Not a loop.
make pre-pr is missing check-scripts
Zero recorded CI failures attributable to the gap.
Fail-open authz paths in the server
All already fixed in committed code — with the exact test the finding proposed adding.
Fourteen further findings
Mostly self-citation of this session’s own workflow files, inflated recurrence counts from one incident described several times, or fixes already shipping on origin/main.

name: feedback-absence-needs-origin-main-grep
description: "Absence is NEVER proven by grep on a working tree — prove non-existence with `git fetch -q origin && git grep <pattern> origin/main` (measured 2026-07-29: 7 sessions made a wrong call from this)"
metadata:
  node_type: memory

---

Measured across 1,209 transcripts (2026-07-29): **7 distinct sessions reached a wrong conclusion by
grepping a working tree to prove code did NOT exist.** The worst case (2026-07-28) drove a wrong
orphaned-script deletion off a "zero callers" grep against a checkout 20 commits stale.

**Why:** `~/Code/lobu` is almost never on `main` — it sits on a feature branch (at time of writing,
`feat/activity-memory-split`, with local `main` 14 commits behind `origin/main`). A plain `grep`/`rg`
there reads whatever branch happens to be checked out, plus uncommitted edits, plus 20+ sibling
worktrees under `.claude/worktrees/`. A hit proves existence; a MISS proves nothing at all.

**How to apply:** to assert code does not exist, run

    git fetch -q origin && git grep <pattern> origin/main

The `fetch` is load-bearing — `origin/main` itself goes stale between sessions, and this is exactly the
class of error where a stale ref reproduces the original mistake. Applies to EVERY existence check:
the deletion-evidence rule ([[feedback-structural-not-usage-deletion-evidence]]), "is this API still
called", "did that guard ship", and any "no other instance of this bug" claim
([[feedback-generalize-fix-then-grep-class]]).

Corollary: a `grep` hit inside `.claude/worktrees/` is someone else's in-flight branch, not main.

Related trap: [[reference-empty-worktree-node-modules-resolves-main]] — the same "I searched and it
wasn't there" failure with a different root cause.

---
name: feedback-guards-must-assert-coverage
description: "A guard with a continue/early-return skip path must assert its own coverage count — found a live authz guard skipping 75/128 SDK methods while CI reported green (2026-07-29)"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
---

**A guard that can silently skip is not a guard — it is a green light.**

Found live on `origin/main` (2026-07-29) in
`packages/server/src/auth/__tests__/access-model-cross-check.test.ts:130`:
`if (runtimeTier === null) continue;`. Instrumenting the committed file gave
`{noTool:41, manage:9, silentlySkipped:25, total:128}` with `Tests 3 passed` — **75 of 128 SDK methods
were never asserted** while CI reported the authz drift guard green. Hiding in the 25 silently-skipped
methods were **11 real authorization drifts**: `authProfiles.get` declared `read` while the runtime
enforces `admin`, plus `entitySchema.create/update/delete{Type,RelType}` and `feeds.create/update/delete`
all declared `write` against an `admin` runtime. The declared access model was advertising WEAKER
requirements than the runtime enforces.

**How to apply:**
1. Any guard loop with `continue` / early-return must assert its own coverage — an **enumerated
   allowlist** of the known-skipped cases, so a NEW skip fails the build and adding one is a deliberate,
   reviewable act.
2. Do NOT assert `skipped === 0` when a legitimate fallback exists (here, a handler `readOnly` hint the
   static test genuinely cannot reproduce) — a bare zero fails on day one and gets reverted.
3. **Verify a mutation test actually LANDED before trusting red/green.** The `perl -0pi -e` recipe in
   [[feedback-mutation-test-new-tests]] silently no-ops on a whitespace mismatch — a session was fooled
   into "passing" a mutation that was never applied. Re-read the file and confirm red.

Same shape observed in five other subsystems (reconcile, approval, connector ACL, a null no-op path),
so treat it as a class per [[feedback-generalize-fix-then-grep-class]]: on the first hit, grep every
other guard for bare `continue` in an assertion loop.

Generalizes [[feedback-test-the-shape-production-throws]]: a suite is only as strong as the assertions
it actually reaches, and "N tests passed" says nothing about N's denominator.

---
name: reference-org-composite-pk-scoping
description: "Ids on agents/agent_users/grants/agent_secrets/conversations are unique only WITHIN an org — make organizationId required at the resolver seam; a SQL-regex CI guard does NOT work here"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
---

**Design rule, not an open vulnerability.** Several tables use a composite primary key:
`agents_pkey PRIMARY KEY (organization_id, id)` — same shape for `agent_users`, `grants`,
`agent_secrets`, `conversations` (baseline.sql). So a slug like `lobu-builder` shares ONE id across
~20 orgs. An id alone does not identify a row.

**Why this keeps recurring:** it has been fixed one sibling at a time across **8 merged PRs in 3 months**
in disjoint files — #1771, #1772, #1779, #1783, #1784, #1848, #2176 ("Recent listed the wrong org's
threads"), #2181. The body of #2181 literally opens *"Problem (sibling of #2176)"* — i.e.
[[feedback-generalize-fix-then-grep-class]] failing AFTER it was already written down. Each fix was
diff-scoped, so the reviewer only ever found the next instance.

**How to apply:** every read and every delete keyed on such an id must carry `organization_id`. An
org-less fallback branch, or an ownership-first resolve, is a cross-tenant leak rather than a
convenience. The durable fix is structural — make `organizationId` a **required parameter at the
resolver seam** (as #1848 and #1784 each did by hand) so the type system refuses the unscoped call.

**Two corrections worth carrying (do not re-panic about these):**
- **A SQL-regex CI guard in `check-security-patterns.sh` would NOT catch this.** The leaks lived in
  ambient org resolution and TypeScript signatures, not in tagged SQL templates; 44 non-test `agent_id`
  matches would fire as false positives. Enforce at the resolver type, not by grepping SQL — same lesson
  as [[feedback-text-matcher-is-never-the-boundary]].
- **#1848's cross-tenant DELETE was largely a false alarm** — [[project-slack-workspace-fencing-prs]]
  records the fenced handler as dead code. Treat this entry as a design invariant to uphold, not as a
  live prod vulnerability to hotfix.

---
name: feedback-compact-pr-status-and-ci-logs
description: "gh pr checks --required instead of --json statusCheckRollup (8.7x smaller); fetch a CI job log ONCE to a file with --log and grep -a (measured: 170 redundant refetches across 21 sessions)"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
---

Two measured habits from the 2026-07-29 transcript sweep, both about re-fetching things already in hand.

**1. Stop requesting `statusCheckRollup`.** `gh pr view --json` accounts for 761 KB over 325 calls in 40
sessions — 492 KB of that is specifically the `statusCheckRollup` field, which returns the full per-check
array when the only real question is "are the required checks green". Measured live on PR 2280:

    gh pr view 2280 --json ...statusCheckRollup          # 7,520 bytes
    gh pr view 2280 --json number,title,isDraft,mergeStateStatus,reviewDecision   # 182 bytes
    gh pr checks 2280 --required                         # 679 bytes

861 bytes vs 7,520 — **8.7x smaller and more legible** (one line per required check, `pi-review` verdict
inline). Note [[project-make-review-verdict-reality]] currently says to use `statusCheckRollup` before
merging; prefer the compact pair above instead.
Honest scoping: this is ~3.6% of the 21.2 MB tool-result corpus — it leads its peer group, not the
corpus. Worth doing because the fix is one line, not because it moves the needle much.

**2. Fetch a CI job log ONCE, to a file.** 21 sessions made **170 redundant `gh run view … --log*`
fetches on job ids already pulled in the same session.** Worst case hit one job **9 times in 105
seconds**, ending with `--log 2>&1 | sed -n '12510,12540p'` — a full remote re-download of a 12,500-line
log to read 30 lines by offset. Another made 5 calls on one job over 2m23s with `grep -a` appearing only
on the 4th attempt, proving the encoding was never inspected.

**How to apply:**

    gh run view --job <id> --log > /tmp/ci-<id>.log    # once, then grep the file

- Use `--log`, **NOT `--log-failed`** — the latter is empty for non-test job failures (check-drift,
  publish-packages), and that emptiness is exactly what triggers the second fetch.
- `grep` needs **`-a`**: logs are timestamp+ANSI prefixed and read as binary.
- Strip the prefix once with `sed 's/^[^Z]*Z //'` rather than re-fetching a "cleaner" view.

Both are now repo policy (AGENTS.md "Session efficiency" + a docs/GOTCHAS.md "CI triage" section).
See also [[feedback-session-context-bloat-habits]].

Four programs sit on an "OWED prod verify" line with no closure entry:
[[project-mcp-client-activity-surface]] (marked COMPLETE 2026-07-28),
[[project-prod-mcp-reliability-sweep]] (PRs #1980–#1985, 2026-07-15),
[[project-approval-live-state-interaction-contract]], and multi-replica interaction-card loss.

**The diagnosis to reject:** it is NOT that the 30–60 min Flux rollout ([[project-prod-flux-image-automation]])
outlives the session. That was already solved — on 2026-07-14 a session used a self-rescheduling
`ScheduleWakeup` that polled `kubectl exec … grep '^APP_GIT_SHA='` plus
`git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha>`, ran the live check the moment the rollout landed, and edited memory
to "FULLY E2E-VERIFIED on prod". `ScheduleWakeup` appears in 19 sessions but almost entirely for CI/PR
polling. **The working pattern exists and is applied inconsistently because it was written down nowhere.**

**How to apply** — when a merged PR touches a prod-visible surface, before ending the turn:
1. Set a self-rescheduling `ScheduleWakeup` (~1500s) whose prompt carries BOTH the rollout gate (deployed
   SHA → `git merge-base --is-ancestor`) and the specific checks from the PR body.
2. On landing, run the live check, then write the verdict back into the program's memory file as a
   closure line. A program with no closure line is unverified, regardless of what its status says.

**Do NOT build a `prod-verify` GitHub issue queue or a cron agent for this.** Memory already carries
closures fine elsewhere ([[project-slack-workspace-fencing-prs]], [[project-conversation-tools-pr]],
[[project-sidebar-nav-runtime-cred-fields]]); the gap is the habit, not the infrastructure.

Note AGENTS.md gates e2e PRE-merge but said nothing about post-deploy until this was added to
"Ship a change". Distinct from [[feedback-e2e-verification-required]], which covers the pre-merge side.
Exclude human-blocked items (e.g. Slack Grid needs the user to install) — those are not context-loss.

Seven of eight clean — spaces, quotes, malformed JSON, empty stdin all handled, exit 0 throughout, no hangs.

Two findings the workflow's verifier missed:

**Symlink is silent when it should nudge.** A symlink to a 2.4MB PNG produces no warning — `stat -f%z` returns the link's own size (~90 bytes), not the target's. Minor, but it's a gap.

Realistically PATH is never empty, so this is theoretical — but the verifier claimed it tested this case and passed it, which it evidently didn't.

Six changes. Five new entries plus a surgical amendment to `feedback_session_context_bloat_habits.md` rather than a competing duplicate.

The reviewer caught a real logic bug in my own instruction — and it's a good one.

I told the agent to write "poll deployed SHA, then `git merge-base --is-ancestor`." But this repo squash-merges. A squash creates a **new commit** with no ancestry link to the branch head, so testing the *branch* commit against the deployed SHA always exits 1. The gate would never open. The reviewer reproduced it on PR #2280: branch head `06f9b457d` and squash commit `77c3e8a81` have identical trees, but the ancestry check fails.

That's my error propagating from the audit through my brief into the docs. Let me verify the claim myself before fixing.

---
name: reference-squash-merge-breaks-ancestry-checks
description: "A squash merge writes a NEW commit with no ancestry link to the branch — `git merge-base --is-ancestor <branch-head> <deployed>` exits 1 forever even when the trees are identical; resolve the merge SHA via `gh pr view --json mergeCommit`"

---

This repo merges with `--squash` ([[feedback-pr-review-merge-flow]]). A squash merge **creates a new
commit whose parent is `main`, not your branch** — so your branch head is NOT an ancestor of anything on
main, no matter how identical the content is.

**Proved by hand 2026-07-29 on PR #2280:**

    branch head 06f9b457d  tree 0bbadc8a4f866fe6f833f4ccb4dad83b9f61e74f
    squash commit 77c3e8a81  tree 0bbadc8a4f866fe6f833f4ccb4dad83b9f61e74f   # IDENTICAL tree
    git merge-base --is-ancestor 06f9b457d 77c3e8a81   -> exit 1

**Why it bites:** any "has my change deployed yet?" gate written against the branch head **silently never
opens** — it does not error, it just waits forever. This is the failure mode a rollout poller is least
likely to notice, because "not yet deployed" and "structurally impossible" look identical from outside.
Caught by `make review` as a blocker on PR #2282, in a doc line I had written myself about verifying prod.

**How to apply — resolve the squash SHA, then check ancestry in the right order:**

    MERGE_SHA=$(gh pr view <n> --json mergeCommit --jq .mergeCommit.oid)
    git merge-base --is-ancestor "$MERGE_SHA" "$DEPLOYED_SHA"   # merge commit FIRST

Two independent ways to get this wrong, both silent:
1. **Wrong commit** — branch head instead of the squash commit. Never opens.
2. **Wrong argument order** — reversed, it asks "is the deploy an ancestor of my commit", which **accepts
   a stale deploy** and reports success before the change shipped.

Now encoded as step 10 of "Ship a change" in AGENTS.md. Pairs with
[[feedback-post-merge-prod-verify-wakeup]] (the wakeup pattern this gate rides on) and
[[feedback-absence-needs-origin-main-grep]] (the other "git told me nothing, so I concluded the wrong
thing" trap). Generalizes: **a check that can only ever return one answer is not a check** — see
[[feedback-guards-must-assert-coverage]].

## Device-connector bug: fully diagnosed from prod

Not vague at all once I pulled the real error field — my first pass only captured `msg` and missed `err`.

**Root cause.** The unique index is on `(organization_id, connector_key, device_worker_id)`. But `ensureDeviceConnectorWired` looks a connection up by `(org, connector, auth_profile_id IS NULL)` with `ORDER BY id ASC LIMIT 1` — it never considers `device_worker_id`. Then `reconcilePin` does a bare `UPDATE ... SET device_worker_id = target` with **no guard** against another live row already holding that device.

**Confirmed in prod data:**

```
org 8dc12bdd — apple.computer_use, 2 live rows, 2 distinct devices
  397  mac-computer-use          → device 2c295bed…   (2026-07-05)
  447  mac-computer-use-buremba  → device e7806c72…   (2026-07-22)
```

The lookup always picks 397, tries to pin it to the device 447 holds, violates the index, aborts the transaction. 21/21 errors were this exact string. Every poll, forever — a permanent failure, not a transient race.

Worth noting the source comment at the insert claims an advisory lock makes this unraceable. Prod disagrees, and the comment is reasoning about slug collisions on a *different* key than the one that actually fires. There is **zero** `ON CONFLICT` handling anywhere in the file.

I wrote a 3-case reproducing test — the collision, the guarded fix, and the normal-pin path to prove the guard doesn't break the happy case. It needs a real DB, so I stood up a throwaway pg18 + pgvector on port 55432 rather than pointing at the shared remote `owletto` database your memory warns about. The harness has its own guard requiring "test" in the DB name, which would have blocked me anyway.

First red run failed on `@lobu/core` resolution — the empty-worktree stale-dist trap, also from your memory. Building now.

**Org-scoping diagnosis** is running read-only in parallel; I'll report what it finds rather than predicting it.

**Not touching prod data.** Rows 397/447 are a real user's connections; per your rule I'll surface them for your decision rather than deleting anything.

---

## ROOT CAUSE

**Not a missing parameter — a store layer that treats "no org" as "no filter."** `packages/core/src/agent-store.ts:109-128` defines `AgentConfigStore` with **every method taking only `agentId`** — there is no org parameter in the contract at all. Org is supplied out-of-band via an AsyncLocalStorage ambient (`packages/server/src/lobu/stores/org-context.ts:8-19`). The Postgres implementation then splits on whether that ambient happens to be set, and **the write methods and read methods make opposite choices**:

- Writes call `getOrgId()`, which **throws** when unset: `postgres-stores.ts:164, 197, 236, 288, 317, 335, 343, 416`.
- Reads call `tryGetOrgId()`, which returns null and drops the `organization_id` predicate entirely: `postgres-stores.ts:135-158` (`getSettings`), `217-230` (`getMetadata`), `361-377` (`getConnection`), `535-538` (`deleteConnection`).

The load-bearing bug is the comment at **`postgres-stores.ts:131-134`**, still on `origin/main` today:

```
// Workers/gateway-internal callers run without org context — agent IDs
// are globally unique and the worker token already proves authenticity,
// so falling back to id-only lookup is safe.
```

"agent IDs are globally unique" is **false** — `agents_pkey PRIMARY KEY (organization_id, id)` (`db/migrations/00000000000000_baseline.sql:2692`). That single stale invariant is the generator of all 8 PRs. `SELECT ... FROM agents WHERE id = ${agentId}` (`postgres-stores.ts:157`, `229`) returns an **arbitrary** row among ~20 for `lobu-builder`, silently, with no error and no log.

The same silent-degrade shape is templated into a reusable helper: `orgScope()` at `org-context.ts:52-54` returns `sql\`\`` (empty fragment) when orgId is null, and is used unguarded at `grant-store.ts:144, 189, 215, 249` — including on a `DELETE` (`revoke`, line 244-250). `user-agents-store.ts:48-53, 71-75` hand-rolls the identical org-less branch.

**Why it recurs one sibling at a time:** because the org isn't in the type, a caller cannot be checked. The compiler is satisfied by `getSettings(agentId)`. The only signal that a call site is wrong is a human tracing whether an ambient happens to be established on that specific dispatch path — which is why the fix has landed 53 times as `orgContext.run({organizationId}, …)` wrappers scattered across 26 files, each one a manual re-establishment of the ambient at a call site rather than a fix at the store.

**A second, distinct root cause** accounts for #2176 and #2181 only: `verifyOwnedAgentAccess` in `routes/shared/agent-ownership.ts:94-203` is an authorization function that also *emits* `organizationId` (`AgentOwnershipResult.organizationId`, line 22). For a per-org **system** agent, "which org authorizes you" ≠ "which org are you viewing" — `resolveAuthorizedOrgId` (line 78-92) returns the caller's *ownership* org from `agent_users`, which for the Builder is their personal org, not the `x-lobu-org` workspace. #2176 and #2181 fixed this by inverting the precedence to ambient-first (`agent-history.ts:429, 446-459` and `506-507, 522-528`). This is a **tenant-selection** bug, not an unfiltered-query bug.

---

## IS THE PROPOSED FIX RIGHT?

**Partially — and as literally stated, unimplementable.** Three problems:

1. **There is no single "resolver seam."** The audit's phrasing assumes one. There are at least four independent id→row resolvers with no common chokepoint:
   - `createPostgresAgentConfigStore` (`postgres-stores.ts:127-355`) — `agents`
   - `GrantStore` (`gateway/permissions/grant-store.ts:122-252`) — `grants`
   - `UserAgentsStore` (`gateway/auth/user-agents-store.ts:34-120`) — `agent_users`
   - `PostgresSecretStore` (`lobu/stores/postgres-secret-store.ts:87-197`) — `agent_secrets`
   
   They share the `org-context.ts` *helpers* but not a function. A "make organizationId required at the resolver seam" PR has no single file to land in.

2. **It does not cover #2176/#2181 at all.** Those two callers already *had* an org — they passed the **wrong one**. A required parameter would have been satisfied by `result.organizationId` and the bug would still ship. Since #2181's body literally names itself a sibling of #2176, and the audit was meant to explain the recurrence, missing the pair that motivated the audit is a material gap.

3. **`resolveOrgId` / `orgScope` would survive it.** Making the parameter required at `AgentConfigStore` still leaves `resolveOrgId(explicit) → explicit ?? tryGetOrgId()` (`org-context.ts:29-31`) and `orgScope(sql, null) → sql\`\`` (`org-context.ts:52-54`) intact. A required-but-`string | undefined`-satisfiable parameter that flows into `orgScope` reproduces the exact same unfiltered query with a green typecheck.

**What is right about it:** putting org in the type is directionally correct and is the only thing that makes call sites *checkable*. It's necessary. It is not sufficient, and it's not the smallest first move.

---

## REMAINING SITES

**Tier 1 — unfiltered query on a composite-PK table (real cross-tenant read):**
- `packages/server/src/lobu/stores/postgres-stores.ts:148-158` — `getSettings` org-less branch, `WHERE id = $1`
- `packages/server/src/lobu/stores/postgres-stores.ts:225-230` — `getMetadata` org-less branch, `WHERE id = $1`
- `packages/server/src/gateway/permissions/grant-store.ts:129,144` — `hasGrant`, `orgScope` empty ⇒ cross-org grant satisfies a check
- `packages/server/src/gateway/permissions/grant-store.ts:177,189` — `isDenied`
- `packages/server/src/gateway/permissions/grant-store.ts:208,215` — `listGrants`
- `packages/server/src/gateway/permissions/grant-store.ts:242,249` — `revoke` — **`DELETE` with no org predicate**; same cross-tenant wipe primitive #1848 closed for bindings
- `packages/server/src/gateway/auth/user-agents-store.ts:48-53` — `removeAgent` org-less `DELETE FROM agent_users`
- `packages/server/src/gateway/auth/user-agents-store.ts:71-75` — `listAgents` org-less branch

**Tier 2 — callers with a reachable org that don't pass one:**
- `packages/server/src/gateway/cli/gateway.ts:392-396` — `ownsAgent(platform, userId, agentId)`, 4th arg omitted; #1848 added it to the history routes (`agent-history.ts:448-453, 523-528`) but not here
- `packages/server/src/gateway/cli/gateway.ts:401` — `getMetadata(agentId)` in the same auth path
- `packages/server/src/gateway/routes/public/agent.ts:858` — `ownershipMetadataStore.getMetadata(agentId)` feeding `tokenOrganizationId`; ambient here is the caller's **default** org, while `workspaceScopedOrgId` (line 830-832) is already computed 26 lines above and not used for this read
- `packages/server/src/gateway/routes/public/agent.ts:807` — `getMetadata(DEFAULT_AGENT_ID)`; mitigated by the `!== callerOrgId` check on line 810, so read-only leak is contained
- `packages/server/src/gateway/auth/mcp/proxy.ts:477` — `getMetadata(agentId)` on the guardrail-trip audit path, explicitly reached when `tokenData.organizationId` is absent (line 475); mislabels the security audit record
- `packages/server/src/catalog/installed.ts:131` — `configStore.getSettings(agentId)`; relies on `runWithWorkerOrgContext` per #1784's audit — correct *today*, fragile, no assertion
- `packages/server/src/lobu/agent-routes.ts:545, 1242, 1245, 1288, 1327, 1572, 2012` — request-path, ambient set by `api-auth-middleware.ts:70`; correct today, unasserted

Tier-1 count: **8**. Tier-2 count: **~13**.

**Explicitly NOT a site:** `postgres-secret-store.ts:87-197` degrades to a *sentinel* (`GLOBAL_ORG_ID`), never to an unfiltered query, and logs loudly on the write paths (lines 131-141, 160-165). That is the correct pattern already present in the codebase.

---

## RECOMMENDED PLAN

**PR 1 — smallest safe first move (start here).** Kill the silent degrade in the shared helper, not the signatures. In `org-context.ts`: make `orgScope(sql, null)` **throw** rather than return an empty fragment, and add `orgScopeOrGlobal()` for the deliberate all-tenant callers. Then fix the 8 Tier-1 sites to either pass an org or opt in explicitly. Zero signature changes, zero call-site churn, and it converts every future instance of this bug from a silent cross-tenant read into a startup/test failure. `grant-store.ts:242-250` (`revoke` DELETE) is the highest-severity single line and lands in this PR.

**PR 2 — same treatment at the store.** Replace the org-less branches at `postgres-stores.ts:148-158` and `225-230` with the `listConnections` guard already in the same file (`postgres-stores.ts:393-399`: log + return empty). That pattern is prod-proven, and it deletes the false comment at lines 131-134. Still no signature change.

**PR 3 — the type change, via the overload sequencing you proposed.** Add `getSettingsScoped(agentId, organizationId)` / `getMetadataScoped(...)` to `AgentConfigStore` (`core/src/agent-store.ts:109-128`), migrate the ~21 Tier-1+Tier-2 call sites, then delete the unscoped originals. Do this *after* PR 1-2 so migration mistakes fail loudly instead of silently. Blast radius is modest — 21 direct call sites plus 3 implementations (`postgres-stores.ts`, `in-memory-agent-store.ts`, `base-agent-store.ts`) — but the 53 `orgContext.run` wrappers become deletable, which is the real payoff.

**PR 4 — the second root cause, independent of 1-3.** Split `AgentOwnershipResult.organizationId` (`agent-ownership.ts:22`) into two fields: `authorizingOrganizationId` (which org vouches for you) and drop the implicit "and this is also the org to query." Force callers to name the target tenant. This is what #2176/#2181 did by hand in one file; generalizing it prevents the third sibling.

**Do not** attempt PR 3 as the first PR. It is the change the prior audit proposed, and landing it first gives you the largest diff with the weakest safety net — a mis-migrated call site passing `undefined` into `resolveOrgId` is indistinguishable from a correct one until PR 1 exists.

---

## CONFIDENCE

**86.**

Read directly on `origin/main`: all 8 PR bodies and file lists; `org-context.ts` in full; `postgres-stores.ts:1-400, 525-541`; `grant-store.ts:95-268`; `user-agents-store.ts:1-121`; `agent-store.ts:90-181`; `agent-ownership.ts` in full; `agent-settings-store.ts:60-171`; `agent-history.ts:395-570`; `agents.ts:40-215`; `agent.ts:795-880`; `postgres-secret-store.ts:80-200`; `mcp/proxy.ts:440-490`; the baseline PK constraints; and ripgrep enumerations of `orgScope`/`resolveOrgId`/`tryGetOrgId`/`orgContext.run`/`getSettings(`/`getMetadata(`/`ownsAgent(`.

High confidence (95+) on: the root cause and the `postgres-stores.ts:131-134` false invariant; the non-existence of a single resolver seam; #2176/#2181 being a separate root cause the proposal doesn't address; the Tier-1 list.

**Weaker, labeled:** Tier-2 reachability is **inferred** — I confirmed the ambient is set at `api-auth-middleware.ts:70` and `proxy-shared.ts:141`, and relied on #1784's stated sweep for the tool path, but did not trace every dispatch path myself. Some Tier-2 entries may be provably safe. The blast-radius count (~21) is grep-derived and excludes the `packages/owletto` submodule, which several PRs touched and I did not enter.</result>

**No, I'm not sure — and now I know it's wrong.**

The fast path at line 105 is a *completely separate* query. It `LEFT JOIN connections` on `(org, connector, auth_profile_id IS NULL)`, `GROUP BY c.id`, `LIMIT 1` — with **no ORDER BY at all**. So `readyConnectionId` is whichever row Postgres happens to return.

That path calls `reconcilePin` at 211/215 and then `return`s — it never reaches the lookup at line 284 I proposed fixing. On prod, `apple.computer_use` is fully wired, so it takes the fast path every poll. **My fix would not have executed.** I'd have shipped a change, watched the error keep firing, and been baffled.

content.text:
No — I was wrong twice, and the second answer was worse than the first.

## What I got wrong

**My "verified" fix targets dead code.** There are three `reconcilePin` call sites, not one. I only read the slow path (line 366). Lines 211/215 are a **fast path** with its own separate query that `LEFT JOIN`s connections with **no ORDER BY at all**, then `return`s — never reaching the lookup I proposed changing.

And prod takes that fast path. `apple.computer_use` has `feeds_schema = {}`, so `declaredFeedKeys = []`, so the `ready` check short-circuits true on every poll. My device-first ORDER BY would have sat in code this connector never executes. I'd have shipped it, watched the error continue, and had no idea why.

My "verification" was a toy table with hand-written SQL. It proved my hypothesis was self-consistent — not that it touched the failing path. Same mistake as the first fake reproducer, one level up.

**The second fix was worse.** Release-then-pin runs clean, so I nearly took it. Then I looked at the rows:

```
397  mac-computer-use          private  device 2c295bed  updated 2026-07-06
447  mac-computer-use-buremba  org      device e7806c72  updated 2026-07-28
```

397 is a three-week-old abandoned relic. 447 is org-visible and was updated **yesterday** — it's the live connection. Release-then-pin would strip the working device off 447 and unpin it, breaking a setup in active use to silence a log line. Mechanically green, functionally destructive.

## Where that leaves it

The error is real and reproduced. But the fix isn't a SQL tweak, because the actual defect is a **contract violation**: the fast-path query assumes one connection per `(org, connector)` — no ORDER BY, `LIMIT 1` — while the schema deliberately permits one per *device*, exactly like `idx_connections_org_connector_account_live` does for OAuth accounts. `manage_connections` already handles this correctly with a device-keyed pre-flight check whose comment says it exists to avoid hitting the index "as a primary exception." `device-reconcile.ts` never got that treatment on either path.

A correct fix has to make **both** queries device-aware and decide what "the connection for this connector" means when several exist — and that's a design question about whether 397 should be tombstoned, not a query I can quietly rewrite.

I'm not going to guess a third time. Two candidate fixes looked verified and were wrong, both because I tested my hypothesis instead of the production path.

What I'd want before writing code: your call on whether 397 is garbage to retire (making this partly a data problem with a much smaller code fix), or whether multi-device-per-connector is a real supported shape that both queries must handle properly. That's the fork, and it's yours — I'd be inventing product intent if I picked.
you can use workflows to be smarter if you need

Fair — but I should be precise about what a workflow can and can't resolve here. Two of my three failures came from not reading enough code, which parallel agents genuinely help with. The third came from a product question no amount of compute answers.

Let me use it for the part it fits: independent readings of the actual failing path, with the explicit job of refuting my current understanding.

export const meta = {
  name: 'device-pin-root-cause',
  description: 'Independently determine the correct fix for the device-pin unique violation, with adversarial refutation of the leading hypothesis',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Investigate', detail: 'four independent lenses on the failing path' },
    { title: 'Refute', detail: 'attack each proposal for dead-code and destructive-write failure modes' },
    { title: 'Decide', detail: 'synthesize into one recommendation plus the open product question' },
  ],
}

const REPO = '/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu'
const FILE = 'packages/server/src/worker-api/device-reconcile.ts'

const FACTS = `
ESTABLISHED FACTS — verified by direct observation, do NOT re-litigate these, build on them:

1. PROD ERROR (21x in 10 min, ongoing): "[device-connectors] Failed to wire device connector" with
   err = 'duplicate key value violates unique constraint "idx_connections_org_connector_device_live"',
   connectorKey='apple.computer_use'. Swallowed by a catch, so it retries forever.

2. THE INDEX: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_connections_org_connector_device_live ON connections
   (organization_id, connector_key, device_worker_id) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL AND device_worker_id IS NOT NULL.
   It sits directly beside idx_connections_org_connector_account_live, the same partial-unique pattern
   keyed on account_id — where multiple connections per (org, connector) is EXPLICITLY intended, one per account.

3. PROD DATA (org 8dc12bdd, connector apple.computer_use, both live, both pinned):
     id=397  slug=mac-computer-use          visibility=private  device=2c295bed...  updated 2026-07-06
     id=447  slug=mac-computer-use-buremba  visibility=org      device=e7806c72...  updated 2026-07-28
   Both have ZERO active feeds. Same created_by user. 397 is ~3 weeks stale; 447 was updated yesterday.

4. connector_definitions for apple.computer_use: feeds_schema = {} (so declaredFeedKeys = []),
   required_capability='computer_use', runtime IS NOT NULL.

5. THREE reconcilePin call sites in ${FILE}: lines ~211 and ~215 (FAST PATH) and ~366 (slow path).
   Because declaredFeedKeys is empty, the fast-path 'ready' check short-circuits TRUE, so prod takes
   the FAST PATH every poll and RETURNS before reaching the slow-path lookup at ~line 284.

6. The fast-path query (~line 105) LEFT JOINs connections ON (org, connector, auth_profile_id IS NULL,
   deleted_at IS NULL), GROUP BY c.id, LIMIT 1, with NO ORDER BY — so which of the two rows becomes
   readyConnectionId is arbitrary.

7. reconcilePin's two WHERE guards both constrain ONLY the row being updated (id = connectionId).
   Neither checks whether a DIFFERENT row already holds the target device. Reproduced at SQL level:
   the exact production predicates against the exact prod row shape produce the exact error.

8. The function's own docstring says: "A pin to a device that's still in the fresh set is treated as
   deliberate and never overridden; a pin to a device that has dropped out is repaired (to the sole
   remaining fresh device, or NULL) so the connection keeps running."

9. manage_connections/handlers/crud.ts:~1094 ALREADY does a device-keyed pre-flight duplicate check,
   with a comment saying it exists so callers get a clean error "instead of hitting the partial unique
   index as a primary exception". device-reconcile.ts does NOT do this on either path.

THREE HYPOTHESES ALREADY TRIED AND REJECTED (do not re-propose without new evidence):
 (a) Add NOT EXISTS guard to reconcilePin's UPDATE → makes it a silent no-op, SUPPRESSES the documented
     stale-pin repair. Trades a loud failure for a silent one.
 (b) Device-first ORDER BY in the SLOW-path lookup (~line 284) → DEAD CODE for this connector; prod
     never reaches that line because the fast path returns first.
 (c) Release-then-pin (NULL out the other row's device, then pin) → DESTRUCTIVE. Would strip the live
     device off row 447 (org-visible, updated yesterday) to satisfy stale row 397.

CRITICAL METHOD: the checkout is on a feature branch and local main is stale. To check whether code
exists, ALWAYS 'git fetch -q origin && git grep <pattern> origin/main'. Never conclude "absent" from a
working-tree grep. Read the REAL code at ${REPO}; cite file:line on origin/main.
`

const PROPOSAL_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  additionalProperties: false,
  required: ['finding', 'proposed_fix', 'executes_on_prod_path', 'destructive_risk', 'evidence', 'confidence'],
  properties: {
    finding: { type: 'string', description: 'What you determined, with file:line evidence' },
    proposed_fix: { type: 'string', description: 'Concrete change. If you conclude no code fix is correct, say that instead.' },
    executes_on_prod_path: { type: 'string', description: 'PROVE this fix actually runs on the fast path prod takes. Which line executes it? If it does not, say so.' },
    destructive_risk: { type: 'string', description: 'What could this break? Specifically: does it unpin/steal/delete anything a user relies on?' },
    evidence: { type: 'string', description: 'file:line citations you actually read' },
    confidence: { type: 'integer', description: '0-100' },
  },
}

phase('Investigate')

const LENSES = [
  {
    label: 'fast-path-owner',
    prompt: `${FACTS}

YOUR LENS: the FAST PATH is the only path that matters here. Read ${FILE} lines 100-220 on origin/main exhaustively.

Answer precisely:
- With TWO connection rows matching the LEFT JOIN, what does the query actually return? Does GROUP BY c.id + LIMIT 1 make it nondeterministic, and can it return a row whose device is already held by the other row?
- readyConnectionId is fed straight to reconcilePin. Trace exactly which (row, target) pair produces the violation.
- What is the MINIMAL correct change to the fast path? Consider: making the join device-aware, ordering by device match, or skipping the pin when it cannot be satisfied.
- Does your fix preserve the documented stale-pin REPAIR behavior (fact 8)? Prove it, do not assert it.`,
  },
  {
    label: 'duplicate-origin',
    prompt: `${FACTS}

YOUR LENS: WHY do two rows exist at all? That may be the true defect; the pin violation may be only a symptom.

Investigate on origin/main:
- Which code paths can create a second connections row for the same (org, connector) with auth_profile_id IS NULL? Grep every INSERT INTO connections. Is it manage_connections (user-created), the Mac app, device pairing, or reconcile itself?
- Row 447's slug is 'mac-computer-use-buremba' while 397 is 'mac-computer-use'. What generates that '-buremba' suffix? Find ensureUniqueConnectionSlug and determine what conditions produce a suffixed slug — that is a fingerprint of HOW the duplicate was born.
- Is the duplicate legitimate (two Macs, one connection each — the account_id analogy) or is it a bug that created an orphan?
- If duplicates are legitimate, what SHOULD reconcile do when it finds several? Cite any existing code that already handles multi-row-per-connector correctly.`,
  },
  {
    label: 'house-pattern',
    prompt: `${FACTS}

YOUR LENS: find how the REST of this codebase already solves "pin a device without violating that index", and whether device-reconcile should simply adopt it.

- Read manage_connections/handlers/crud.ts around line 1094 in full. What exactly is its pre-flight check, and what does it do on conflict (clean error? pick the existing one? no-op)?
- git grep origin/main for every other writer of connections.device_worker_id. Include dispatch-chrome-action.ts (it names this index in a constant, CHROME_DEVICE_PIN_UNIQUE — read how it handles the conflict; it apparently used to 500).
- Is there an established idiom (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, pre-flight SELECT, advisory lock, catch-and-degrade)? Name it with file:line.
- Recommend the change that makes device-reconcile consistent with that idiom, and say plainly if the idiom does NOT apply here.`,
  },
  {
    label: 'severity-and-donothing',
    prompt: `${FACTS}

YOUR LENS: be the skeptic. Is a code change even warranted, and what is the actual user-visible harm?

- The error is caught and swallowed. Trace what CONCRETE functionality is broken for the user right now. Does apple.computer_use still work? Both rows have ZERO active feeds and the connector declares feeds_schema={} — so what is the wire pass even accomplishing for this connector? Does the failure matter beyond log noise?
- What breaks if the transaction aborts: does it lose the feed upserts, the definition upsert, the created_by backfill? Read the whole tx body (~lines 250-370) and enumerate what is skipped.
- Would tombstoning the stale row 397 (a DATA fix) resolve it with no code change? What would that break?
- Argue the strongest case for "the right fix is data cleanup plus a guard against recurrence, not a query rewrite". Then argue the strongest case AGAINST that. Be genuinely two-sided.`,
  },
]

const proposals = await parallel(
  LENSES.map((l) => () => agent(l.prompt, { label: l.label, phase: 'Investigate', schema: PROPOSAL_SCHEMA, effort: 'high' }))
)

const live = proposals.filter(Boolean)
log(`${live.length}/${LENSES.length} lenses reported`)

phase('Refute')

const REFUTE_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  additionalProperties: false,
  required: ['survives', 'dead_code_verdict', 'destructive_verdict', 'reason'],
  properties: {
    survives: { type: 'boolean' },
    dead_code_verdict: { type: 'string', description: 'Does the fix actually execute on the fast path prod takes? Quote the line that runs it, or state it is dead code.' },
    destructive_verdict: { type: 'string', description: 'Does it unpin, steal, or delete anything a user depends on? Specifically check row 447.' },
    reason: { type: 'string' },
  },
}

const refuted = await parallel(
  live.map((p, i) => () =>
    agent(
      `${FACTS}

ADVERSARIAL REFUTATION. Another agent proposed this. Your job is to KILL it. Three of my own fixes already died to exactly two failure modes — assume this one has the same disease until proven otherwise.

PROPOSAL: ${JSON.stringify(p)}

Test it against the two killers, by READING THE CODE, not reasoning abstractly:
1. DEAD CODE: prod takes the FAST PATH (facts 4-6) and returns before the slow-path lookup. Does this fix
   run on that path? Name the exact line that executes it. If it only changes slow-path code, it is DEAD
   for apple.computer_use and survives=false.
2. DESTRUCTIVE: does it unpin, steal, or delete anything? Row 447 is org-visible and was updated
   yesterday — any fix that strips its device or deletes it is WRONG, survives=false.
3. Does it suppress the documented stale-pin repair (fact 8)? If it silently no-ops where the code is
   meant to repair, survives=false.
4. Does it actually stop the duplicate-key error, or just move it?

Default to survives=false when uncertain. A killed proposal is a SUCCESS.`,
      { label: `refute:${(p.finding || '').slice(0, 30)}`, phase: 'Refute', effort: 'high', schema: REFUTE_SCHEMA }
    ).then((v) => ({ proposal: p, verdict: v }))
  )
)

const survivors = refuted.filter(Boolean).filter((r) => r.verdict && r.verdict.survives)
log(`${survivors.length}/${refuted.filter(Boolean).length} proposals survived refutation`)

phase('Decide')

const decision = await agent(
  `${FACTS}

You are making the final call for the repo owner. Below are the investigations and the refutation verdicts.

SURVIVED REFUTATION:
${JSON.stringify(survivors, null, 2)}

KILLED (and why — do NOT resurrect these):
${JSON.stringify(refuted.filter(Boolean).filter((r) => r.verdict && !r.verdict.survives).map((r) => ({ fix: r.proposal.proposed_fix, why_killed: r.verdict.reason })), null, 2)}

Write a decision, in plain prose, short:
1. THE CORRECT FIX — the specific change, with file:line. If the honest answer is "data cleanup plus a small guard" or "no code change", say that. If NOTHING survived, say that plainly and explain what the blocker is.
2. WHY the rejected ones were wrong, in one line each.
3. THE OPEN PRODUCT QUESTION the owner must answer before this can ship — specifically: is one-connection-per-DEVICE the intended model (mirroring account_id), or is row 397 simply garbage to retire? Explain what changes depending on the answer.
4. BLAST RADIUS + what test would prove it, red before green, ON THE PATH PROD ACTUALLY TAKES.

Be blunt about uncertainty. Do not manufacture confidence. No preamble.`,
  { label: 'decide', phase: 'Decide', effort: 'high' }
)

return { decision, survived: survivors.length, killed: refuted.filter(Boolean).length - survivors.length }

## What I nailed down while the workflow runs

**The error rate — measured properly this time.** 39 errors across 5 minutes on two pods only 3 minutes old: **~8/min combined**, ongoing, per-replica because both replicas poll independently.

I want to flag a mistake in my own process here. Mid-investigation I told you it was actually "a burst that stopped" — I'd found 19 errors spanning only 157 seconds in a 60-minute window. That was wrong. The window was truncated because the pods had just restarted for the `bff73e8a4` rollout. My original ~3/min reading was right, and the true figure is higher still.

That's the second time this session I've moved off a correct reading by over-reading a short window. The fix is the same one already in your GOTCHAS: check what the window actually covers before drawing a rate from it.

**Neither row is being updated.** `reconcilePin` sets `updated_at = NOW()` on success. Row 397 is 532 hours stale, row 447 is 9.7 hours, and neither has moved while the errors fire. That confirms the transaction aborts every time — no partial success, nothing is being silently half-written.

**On fast-path nondeterminism I have to be honest about what I proved.** The query has no `ORDER BY`, so it carries no ordering *guarantee*. But I tried to force it to return the other row — index hints, disabled seqscan, tuple moves — and it kept returning row 1. So "arbitrary" is correct as a statement about the contract, and unproven as a statement about observed behavior. I'm not going to claim more than I demonstrated.

**What the workflow is doing** is the part I kept getting wrong alone: four independent readings of the actual failing path, then adversarial refutation specifically targeting the two failure modes that killed my previous three attempts — fixes that land in dead code, and fixes that destroy row 447. Each refuter is told to default to "killed" when uncertain.

What it can't settle is the product question: whether one-connection-per-device is the intended model, mirroring `account_id`, or whether 397 is simply garbage to retire. That determines whether this is a query fix or a data cleanup with a small guard, and it's yours to answer — I'd be inventing intent.

## What

`idx_connections_org_connector_device_live` is UNIQUE on `(organization_id, connector_key, device_worker_id)` for live rows, and an org legitimately holds **one connection per device** — the same shape `idx_connections_org_connector_account_live` gives OAuth accounts.

Retiring a Mac leaves its connection pinned to the now-stale device while the replacement Mac's connection holds the only fresh one. The fast path resolves a connection for the `(org, connector)` **with no ORDER BY**, hands it to `reconcilePin`, and the pin UPDATE targets a device the *other* row owns → 23505, the whole wire transaction aborts, and the poll retries forever.

Measured on prod (`summaries-prod`, org `8dc12bdd`, `apple.computer_use`):

```
397  mac-computer-use          private  device 2c295bed (MacBook Pro, last seen 10d)  → STALE
447  mac-computer-use-buremba  org      device e7806c72 (Mac mini,    last seen  2h)  → FRESH
```

Exactly one fresh device ⇒ `matchingDeviceIds.length === 1` ⇒ row 397 is pinned toward the device 447 already holds. **~8 errors/min across two replicas**, swallowed by the catch so it never surfaced.

## Fix

Look up the target device's current owner before pinning; fall back to `NULL` when another live connection holds it. This is the guard `resolveOnlineChromeConnection` **already carries for this same index** — see `findOwnerOf` in `dispatch-chrome-action.ts`, whose comment records that it "used to 500 the dispatcher (multi-Chrome orgs: Mac mini + MacBook)". Same index, same shape, already fixed once for `chrome`; `device-reconcile.ts` was the unfixed sibling.

`NULL` rather than skipping the UPDATE is deliberate: the dead pin is still cleared, so the documented stale-pin repair survives, and an unpinned connection is claimable by any polling device while one pinned to a vanished device is claimable by nobody.

## Red → green

`device-reconcile.ts` had **zero** test coverage. The new integration test drives the real manifest-sourced fast path — a DB-only definition never enters the wire pass, so the connector must arrive via `device_workers.connector_manifests`, exactly as prod's `apple.computer_use` does.

## Class check

Six non-test writers of `device_worker_id`. Two `SET NULL` (cannot violate a partial `IS NOT NULL` index), one is the already-guarded chrome path, one is this fix. **`crud.ts:1866` is a real second instance** — the user-initiated update path has no pre-flight owner check, unlike the create path at `crud.ts:1094`. Filed as a follow-up rather than bundled: it wants a clean user-facing error, not a silent unpin, so it is a different behaviour with a different blast radius.

## Blast radius

---
name: reference_device_pin_unique_index
description: "idx_connections_org_connector_device_live means ONE CONNECTION PER DEVICE (like account_id) — never pin without checking the target device's current owner, and take the autowire advisory lock around that check"
metadata:
  node_type: memory

---

`idx_connections_org_connector_device_live` is UNIQUE on
`(organization_id, connector_key, device_worker_id)` WHERE `deleted_at IS NULL AND device_worker_id IS
NOT NULL`. It sits beside `idx_connections_org_connector_account_live`, the identical pattern keyed on
`account_id` — so **an org legitimately holds one connection PER DEVICE**, exactly as it holds one per
OAuth account. Any code assuming one connection per `(org, connector)` is wrong.

**The prod incident (2026-07-29, fixed in PR #2286).** Retiring a Mac left its connection pinned to the
now-stale device while the replacement Mac's connection held the only fresh one:

    397  mac-computer-use          private  device 2c295bed (MacBook Pro, last seen 10d)  STALE
    447  mac-computer-use-buremba  org      device e7806c72 (Mac mini,    last seen  2h)  FRESH

`ensureDeviceConnectorWired`'s fast path resolves a connection for the (org, connector) **with no ORDER
BY**, handed it to `reconcilePin`, and the pin UPDATE targeted the device row 447 already owned → 23505,
the whole wire transaction aborted, swallowed by the catch, retried forever. **~8 errors/min across two
replicas.** `matchingDeviceIds.length === 1` (only one fresh device) is what makes it fire.

**How to apply — two rules, both load-bearing:**
1. **Never pin without checking the target device's current owner.** Fall back to `NULL`, do NOT skip the
   UPDATE: NULL still clears a dead pin, so the documented stale-pin repair survives, and an unpinned
   connection is claimable by any polling device while one pinned to a vanished device is claimable by
   nobody. Skipping leaves it pinned to a corpse — a silent failure replacing a loud one.
2. **The owner check is read-then-write, so it needs `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('lobu:autowire'),
   hashtext(userId:connectorKey))`.** Verified by hand: without it, two replicas both read "no owner" and
   the second still throws; with it, two concurrent clients complete with zero errors and exactly one row
   pinned. Two of the three `reconcilePin` call sites already had the lock; the third did not.

**This was already solved once and not generalized** — `resolveOnlineChromeConnection` carries
`findOwnerOf` for this same index, its comment recording that it "used to 500 the dispatcher
(multi-Chrome orgs: Mac mini + MacBook)". `device-reconcile.ts` was the unfixed sibling. Textbook
[[feedback_generalize_fix_then_grep_class]]: on the first hit, grep every writer of the column.

**Still unfixed (follow-up):** `manage_connections/handlers/crud.ts:1866`, the user-initiated update
path, has no pre-flight owner check — unlike the create path at `:1094`, which does one specifically to
avoid hitting the index "as a primary exception". It wants a clean user-facing error, not a silent
unpin, so it is a separate behaviour and a separate PR.

**Testing trap that cost three attempts** (see [[feedback_test_the_shape_production_throws]]): a
DB-only `connector_definitions` row does NOT reach the wire pass. `getBundledDeviceConnectors()` reads
the ON-DISK catalog, which is empty in tests, so `byKey` stays empty and the function returns before
pinning anything — the test fails while nothing runs. The connector must arrive via
`device_workers.connector_manifests` (needs `key`, `version`, `name`, `required_capability`,
`runtime.platforms` non-empty, plus `manifest_hash` and `received_at`). Sanity check for any reproducer
here: **the control cases must PASS while only the bug case fails.** All-green or all-red means the
fixture is wrong, not the code.

When two live rows exist and the query returns the one that is *already correctly pinned*, `reconcilePin` no-ops — its `WHERE` requires `device_worker_id IS DISTINCT FROM target` — and the **other** row stays pinned to a vanished device forever. Nothing revisits it.

After #2286 this no longer throws, so it is silent: a retired connection sits pinned to a device that will never poll again, and is claimable by nobody.

Confirmed locally. After `reconcileDeviceCapabilities`, the retired row's `device_worker_id` is still the stale device; expected `NULL`.

Adding a repair-first `ORDER BY` to the fast-path query was tried and **fails**: the ordering keys reference `c.device_worker_id`, which is not in the `GROUP BY`, and the structural limit remains — the fast path pins exactly one connection per poll while two need attention.

The real fix is probably to reconcile **every** live connection for the `(org, connector)` rather than a single arbitrary one, which is a restructure of the fast path rather than a query tweak. Worth confirming the intended cardinality first: is one-connection-per-device the supported model (the index says yes), and should a retired device's connection be unpinned, tombstoned, or left alone?

/**
 * `organization_id` filter as a composable SQL fragment.
 *
 * Fail-closed by construction: `orgId` is required. This used to accept
 * null/undefined and return an EMPTY fragment, which silently dropped the
 * tenant predicate — a cross-tenant read on every SELECT that used it, and a
 * cross-tenant wipe on `GrantStore.revoke`'s DELETE. Nothing signalled it: no
 * error, no log, just a query answering for every org at once.
 *
 * A caller that cannot produce an org must say so explicitly by resolving it
 * with {@link requireOrgId} (which throws and names the caller) rather than
 * passing a nullable through and inheriting an unscoped query.
 */
export function orgScope(sql: ReturnType<typeof getDb>, orgId: string) {
  return sql`AND organization_id = ${orgId}`;
}
